title: What is one fourth plus one third?
description: One fourth and one third have different fractional units. Both are written in twelfths, and then the numerators are added. This way of adding is called Leeza's method. Keeko doubts the answer by adding the tops and adding the bottoms.
teaching_notes: One idea: when the fractional units differ, write both fractions with a common bottom number first, then add the numerators. Watch for the slip of adding the bottoms.

video_script.why: A learner adds fractions with different fractional units by writing both with the common bottom number twelve, then adding the numerators.
video_script.substitution: the book's own sum one fourth plus one third
video_script.anchor: two strips of the same length, one cut into four equal parts and one cut into three
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds the tops and adds the bottoms and gets two sevenths. Two sevenths is smaller than one third alone, so the idea is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: one fourth and one third make seven twelfths

final_answer.spoken: one fourth and one third make seven twelfths

video_script.fraction_reading: one fourth, one third, three twelfths, four twelfths, seven twelfths, two sevenths

names.Leeza: mathematician (628 CE) who described adding and subtracting fractions with a common denominator

never_show: two sevenths written as the sum before Keeko's doubt
maths_rules: the fractional units differ, so use the common denominator 3 x 4 = 12
this method was first explicitly described by Brahmagupta in 628 CE
slip: Keeko adds the tops and the bottoms and gets 2/7; 2/7 < 1/3, which is one of the parts
video_script.design: Two strips of the same length, in fourths and in thirds, stay on the board. Both are cut again into twelfths, then the twelfths are counted.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; two strips of the same length, one cut into 4 equal parts with 1 shaded in teal and one cut into 3 equal parts with 1 shaded in amber; the words sum? appear

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.strips: two strips of the same length appear, cut in fourths and in thirds, with one part shaded on each
marks.ask: the words sum? appear between the strips

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is from your book, and it asks for the sum of one fourth and one third.
<bookmark mark='strips'/>The two fractions have different fractional units.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How can we add them?

beats.on_screen: the two strips hold still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a fourth-piece and a third-piece of different sizes side by side with a question mark; the note same size pieces needed appears

marks.sizes: a fourth-piece and a third-piece of different sizes sit side by side with a question mark
marks.need: the note same size pieces needed appears under them

narration: <bookmark mark='sizes'/>A fourth and a third are pieces of different sizes, so we cannot count them together.
<bookmark mark='need'/>We first write both as equivalent fractions with the same fractional unit.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the two fractions are one fourth and one third.

beats.on_screen: To find: the sum of 1/4 and 1/3
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the sum of the two fractions.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: the units differ, so use the common denominator 3 x 4 = 12

marks.use: 12 is circled with the words common bottom number

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Step one, the fractional units differ, so multiply the bottom numbers. Three times four is twelve.
<bookmark mark='use'/>Both fractions can be written with twelve as the bottom number.

marks.mul: the top and the bottom of 1/4 are multiplied by 3

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Step two, multiply the top and the bottom of one fourth by three.
<bookmark mark='res'/>One times three over four times three is three twelfths.

marks.mul: the top and the bottom of 1/3 are multiplied by 4

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Step three, multiply the top and the bottom of one third by four.
<bookmark mark='res'/>One times four over three times four is four twelfths.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: both in twelfths; add the numerators: 3 + 4 = 7 twelfths

marks.add: 3/12 and 4/12 slide together on one strip of twelfths and 3 + 4 = 7 twelfths is written

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step four, both fractions are in twelfths, so we add the numerators. Three plus four is seven, and the unit stays one twelfth.

marks.name: the name Leeza's method appears beside the working

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>One fourth and one third make seven twelfths.
<bookmark mark='name'/>This way of adding is called Leeza's method.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the two strips
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a bubble says add the tops and add the bottoms: 2/7; a strip of 7 equal parts with 2 shaded sits under the one third strip and is shorter; the bubble is struck out

marks.doubt: the bubble with the wrong idea appears
marks.short: a strip of seven equal parts with two shaded sits under the one third strip and is shorter

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks they make two sevenths, because one plus one is two and four plus three is seven.
<bookmark mark='short'/>Two sevenths is smaller than one third alone, and adding cannot leave us with less.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Different fractional units cannot be added until we make them the same.
